newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Germany rates to Americas steady, business strong.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Germany rates to Americas steady, business strong.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Germany to North America are holding stable after a good start to the summer, a Reuters' survey showed.
But pressure on rates could increase in July as the market enters the traditionally quiet summer months and extra passenger aircraft capacity comes on to the market, industry sources indicated.
Business to Latin America is generally holding steady although marked by regional differences while Africa is continuing to disappoint, managers said.

The latest figures from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Cargo Accounts Settlement System (CASS) show that air cargo yields in Germany fell slightly during March after rising in February.
In April, the total German market volume rose 9.2 percent to nearly 48,000 tonnes, CASS figures showed.

But air cargo exports flown out of Frankfurt airport, the main German gateway, fell back 0.3 percent year-on-year last month, as companies cut production due to the four public holidays in May, airport authority figures revealed.
This "long weekend" effect is likely to have hit air cargo yields in May, market observers pointed out.
Florian Pfaff, Lufthansa Cargo sales manager Germany, said business had been weaker in May after a good first four months for the whole industry.
"May was clearly down due to the holidays but we could not have expected anything else," he noted.
In expectation of lower demand, Lufthansa cancelled several freighter flights last month and sent the aircraft for technical maintenance, he explained.
But Pfaff added: "Our expectations are that the market will be stable. We have good bookings for June and July."
The Germany sales manager of a large European airline added: "The market is fairly stable at the moment and I do not see pressure on rates."
There appeared to be a rise in small shipments although total tonnage was fairly constant, he noted.
Volker Oesau, Danzas intercontinental manager Germany, said he did not expect a summer downturn in air cargo shipments this year.
"I believe the air cargo market has recovered. Exports are growing above expectations and there will be further market growth for the next few months," he said.
The North American market out of Germany grew 21 percent to nearly 17,000 tonnes in April, the latest CASS figures showed.

Several new passenger services aimed at the summer holiday market to the U.S., including daily flights by United Airlines and Continental Airlines, will increase market capacity over the coming weeks.

Andreas Gutberlet, Continental's cargo sales manager Germany, said he would gain an extra 12-15 tonnes of daily freight capacity from July 1 until August 31 with the addition of a second daily Frankfurt-Newark DC10-30 flight.
"We see a relative stabilisation (in rates) through the summer. Whether we need to react depends on our own and market capacity and we will follow the market development closely," he said.
But Gutbertlet stressed he would give agents at least four weeks' advance notice of any change in rates after Continental held rates stable this spring.
Business in May had been marked by ups and downs due to the public holidays although volumes were generally stable, he added.
Lothar Schaller, of managing director of Airlines Sales Association, sales agent for US Airways, said: "The market is good at the moment and I cannot see any summer gap appearing yet."
Lufthansa's Pfaff said demand for air cargo transport to North America had clearly risen because of the favourable dollar exchange rate.
"The North Atlantic is booming and even in May it was good. The market is above last year even with the extra summer capacity," he noted.
Oesau, of Danzas, forecast rates would generally hold to the U.S. even though there could be more spot-pricing.
"Some airlines have reduced U.S. capacity and I believe rates will stay stable," he said.
The South American market out of Germany declined six percent in April to some 3,400 tonnes, the latest CASS figures showed in support of market feeling that Latin America is cooling off at present.
George von Doehren, Iberia sales manager Germany, said: "May was not so good because of the holidays and they did not help us but otherwise there was a slight upwards trend."
Argentina was still a little quiet but consumers were still buying even though less money appeared to be available, he noted.
"There is not the boom which there was but there does not appear to be a particular connection to the economic conditions in the country," he noted.
Iberia believed there would be German demand for its new twice-weekly Madrid-Montevideo flight starting July 4, von Doehren said.
The Chilean market, where Lan Chile with five direct flights a week from Germany was a major competitor, was holding steady at present, he added.
Dieter Uhl, managing director of Air Impact Luftfahrtagentur, GSA for Colombian carrier Avianca, said the airline's sales figures had doubled in May thanks to good demand.
Demand for the flights of Challenge Air, also represented by Air Impact, from Miami to smaller Central and South American destinations was also growing steadily, he added.
"There are no big shipments but the number of small consignments up to one tonne is increasing," Uhl said.
Oesau, of Danzas, said Latin America appeared to be going unevenly with Brazil and Argentina still growing but Colombia and Venezuela declining.
Lufthansa's Pfaff said load factors to Latin America were good at more than 90 percent with Argentina booming but Brazil not so strong as last year.
Lufthansa freighters were full with airfreight from Scandinavia and Italy, he added.
"There is no need to change and we will definitely not change our rates," Pfaff said.
Varig was also seeing good cargo load factors out of Germany to Brazil at present, sources said.
The African market out of Germany rose sharply in April by 30 percent to some 2,100 tonnes, the latest CASS figures showed.
But competition between European and African airlines flying to the main market, South Africa, remains intense with plenty of consolidation freight going via Amsterdam.
Lufthansa's Pfaff noted: "Market growth is there but there is increased competition both within Germany and there is a lot going through Amsterdam.
"We are not satisfied at the moment. Our prices are too high and yield is down."
But Lufthansa would not enter a price war to South Africa despite the substantial differences between German and Dutch air cargo rates.
Pfaff stressed: "I do not want to compete on prices. Capacity will be kept stable and we have no plans to change rates." - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
